Sessions are a projection of these, never the other way round.

seq.description: Monotonic per worker. This is the resume cursor.

oneOf.description:
One line of a session's transcript, whole.

Every event a single log line normalised into, together in one frame.
A line is the only place a client's cursor can be — several events come
from one line, and `ContentDelta` appends rather than replaces, so a
boundary inside a line can neither be resumed from (the rest is lost)
nor re-sent (the text arrives twice). Delivered whole, it is always
exactly one or the other.

items.description:
One thing that happened, and where in the log it was said.

The line number travels with the event because several events can come from
one line, and a client's cursor has to be a position in the agent's log
rather than a count of what it drew.

oneOf.description:
Frames were dropped because this subscription fell behind. Resubscribe
from your cursor; nothing else on the socket is affected.
This subscription cannot be served, and why.

ServerFrame.description:
What the server says.

The two payloads that matter are the ones the SSE endpoints already send,
unchanged: `ft_core::Event` and `ConversationEvent`. This is not a second
event system — it is the same events with a topic on the front, sharing one
connection.

Session.description: A line of work with a conversation attached and a branch at the end.

branch.description:
The first checkout's branch, or `None` for a bare agent.

Every checkout in a session is cut with the same requested name, so this
is the right thing to show once — but git may have numbered them
differently, so anything acting on a branch reads it from the checkout.

checkouts.description:
Every repository checked out into this session's workspace.

Empty for a bare agent. One for most sessions. The whole point of the
list is the third case.

forgottenAt.description:
When it was removed from here without the machine being told.

Set only by a forced removal: the host was not answering, so nobody
could tear the workspace down. The session is `Ended` here from that
moment, and the agent may well still be running there.

maySpeak.description:
Whether whoever asked may speak *in this conversation*.

`may_write` is about the place: it says you can work in this workspace
— add an agent of your own, open a terminal, attach a repository.
This is about the conversation, and it is true only for the person who
started it.

They are separate because what they protect is separate. A workspace is
a directory and can be shared, moved, handed to a team. A conversation
is a running agent authenticated with one person's subscription, and
its turns push with that person's git token under that person's name.
Sharing the room was never meant to hand over the account, and for a
while it did.

mayWrite.description:
Whether whoever asked for this may act in it, or only watch.

**Sent, because it cannot be derived.** The level was deliberately left
off this type once, on the grounds that a client already holds the
directories it can see and can work the answer out from the path. That
stopped being true the moment a single workspace could be shared to one
person by name: an exception lives on the resource, in no directory, so
there is nothing on the client that mentions it.

Without it, a viewer was shown a composer, typed, pressed send, and the
server answered 404 — which the screen reported as "Working — nothing
heard", because an echo had already been added optimistically. A
control that is drawn and then refused is worse than one that is
absent: it reads as the product being broken.

`true` by default so that a client talking to a control plane that
predates this field behaves as it did before, rather than deciding
everybody is a spectator.

name.description:
What to call it. `Agent 3` until somebody says otherwise.

Separate from `title`, which is cut from the prompt and describes the
work. This one identifies the session, which is a different job: five
sessions on one repository all called "Ask me…" are impossible to tell
apart, and renaming one of them to "the flaky test" fixes that.

note.description:
Why it is in that status, when whatever set it knew.

Only ever the agent's own words, and only for the statuses that mean
your move. Cleared when it goes back to working — a question that has
been answered is not worth keeping on screen.

number.description:
Assigned once, never reused, and the same for as long as the session
exists. What `name` is derived from, and what a name that has been
changed can always be traced back to.

owner.description:
Whoever started it.

Everything else about who may do what follows from this: who can open
the session, whose token pushes its branch, whose name goes on its
commits. Carried on the session rather than looked up each time,
because every one of those questions is asked while it is already
loaded.

ownerName.description:
What to call the owner, so a shared list can say whose this is.

Sent because it cannot be looked up: listing the people in an
organisation is an administrator's request, and a member seeing a
colleague's workspace still has to be told a name rather than an id.

path.description:
Which directory the workspace is filed in — `u/kevin/…` for somebody's
own, `d/backend/…` once it has been handed to a directory.

proposedTitle.description:
What the agent proposed calling this work, when it finished.

A draft to edit rather than a box to fill. Nothing acts on it: it is
what the review sheet starts with, and whoever is shipping decides what
it actually says.

pullRequest.description:
Where the pull request is, once one has been opened.

Remembered so a screen can tell "pushed" from "already open" without
asking GitHub, which is what lets one control name the next step rather
than offering every verb at once.

repo.description:
The first checkout's slug, or `None` for a bare agent.

A convenience for the places that want one name — a row in a list, a
caption. [`Session::checkouts`] is what is actually true.

steps.description:
What this session is going to do, in order, decided when it was created.

Here rather than inferred from events so the screen has something to
show before the worker has said a word — the difference between "this
is fetching a repository" and a blank page.

taskKey.description:
Short, derived from the prompt — the prompt itself lives in the transcript.
The task this worktree was cut for, if it came from one.

Source-scoped — `github:acme/web#5138` — so a second tracker cannot
collide with the first. Everything else about the task is read from the
tracker when somebody looks; these two are ours, and they are what lets
the rail show `#5138` and shipping offer to close it.

oneOf.description:
What this session's workspace is taking of its machine, right now.

Not stored. Filled in from what the host last reported, so it is absent
on a session whose worker cannot measure and on one whose first report
has not landed — which the interface draws the same way, as no meters.

SessionId.description: Identifies a session — the unit of work you talk to.

SetIdentity.description: What to sign commits with, typed rather than derived.

key.description: The OpenAI key. Replaces whatever is there; the old one is not recoverable.

SetupState.description:
Which parts of setting up are still outstanding.

Read before anything else, so the interface knows whether to show the
wizard, and how much of it.

completed.description:
Somebody has been through onboarding, however much they skipped.

Once true it stays true: the steps after the organisation exist to point
somewhere, and a tour that reappears every time this page is opened is a
tour nobody finishes twice. Connecting GitHub later is asked for on the
screen that needs it, where there is no skipping it.

needsGithub.description:
No GitHub application is configured. Not a blocker — it is skippable,
and pasting a repository URL works without one.

needsOrganization.description: Nobody has named the organisation yet.

needsPassword.description:
The signed-in account's password was chosen by somebody else and has
to be replaced. The only step of setting up that is not about the
install — it is raised for anybody invited or reset, long after.

publicUrl.description:
Where a person reaches this Firetower in a browser.

**Not whatever host served the page.** The interface and the control
plane are two addresses — in development they are two ports, and in a
deployment behind a proxy they can be two names — so a screen that hands
somebody a sign-in link cannot read it off its own `window.location`
and be right anywhere but the installation it happens to be running on.

`FIRETOWER_PUBLIC_URL` when it is set, and the interface's own address
otherwise. It is the same value the session notifications link to.

Share.description:
How a workspace competes for a machine that two of them want at once.

The other half of [`WorkspaceSize`], and a different question. A size is how
much a workspace may have at most; a share is who yields when both want the
same core in the same moment. Which means a size can be promised in
gigabytes and a share cannot be promised in anything — on a quiet machine
every share gets everything, and this only starts to decide between them
once somebody else is working too.

Here rather than in the worker because both ends read it: the control plane
offers the choice and stores it, and the worker turns it into a number the
kernel understands.

SignIn.description: What a sign-in needs from the caller.

accountId.description: The named account to authenticate. Made first with `create_account`.

hostId.description:
Which host should do it. Any that has the agent, by default.

It matters only in that OpenAI delivers the credential to whichever
machine asked for the code — and that machine hands it straight to us,
so which one it was stops mattering the moment it lands.

region.description:
Which Kimi the account lives on: `global` for kimi.ai, `mainland-cn`
for kimi.com. Omit for the default, and for every other agent.

They are separate account namespaces rather than mirrors, so picking
the wrong one signs a different person in and reports success.

SignedIn.description: What a browser gets for a correct password.

token.description: Sent back on every later request. Said once — only its hash is kept.

SlashCommand.description: A slash command this session offers, as the agent reported it at startup.

oneOf.description:
Let ssh choose: the agent first, then the usual names in `~/.ssh`.

The default, and what an absent `identity_file` used to mean. Still
useful for a control plane running on a machine whose ssh is already
configured — a development install, or a binary on a host.

The key Firetower made for itself, sealed in the vault.

What a server added through the interface uses. Firetower holds this one
because in a container there is no other way for it to hold anything:
it is scoped to this installation, opens nothing else, and is revoked by
deleting one line on one machine.

A private key the operator pasted, sealed in the vault under this name.

For an existing key they would rather reuse, or one signed by a CA.

A path on the machine running the control plane.

Still correct when that machine is not a container. Kept so that every
host added before this existed keeps working and means what it did.

SshKey.description:
Where an agent can run.

Three kinds, and they are not a ladder — each is the right answer sometimes.
Poking at a repository by hand wants the first; leaving an agent running for
an hour wants the third.
Which private key ssh should offer when reaching a server.

This used to be one field, `identity_file`: a path on the machine running the
control plane. That was right while the control plane ran on the operator's
own machine, and stopped being right in a container — the path is read
inside the container, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` names a file that exists on their
machine and not in this one, and no path they can type would bridge the two.

So a host now says *which* key rather than *where* it is, and only one of
these is still a path.

Step.description:
One stage of bringing a session up.

The point of naming them is that the whole list is knowable *before* any of
it runs — so a session can show what it is going to do the moment it is
created, rather than assembling a shape out of events as they arrive. A step
nobody has reached yet is still worth showing.

StoredEnv.description: What was stored, and what was not.

names.description: Every variable this repository now has, in order.

skipped.description:
Lines that were skipped, and why — said rather than swallowed, because
a variable that silently never arrives is a long afternoon.

StreamKind.description:
Which stream a piece of text belongs to.

Separate from [`ItemKind`] because one item can carry more than one: a
command has both its own text and its output.

SubjectKind.description: Whether a grant names one person or a whole team.

Successor.description: Who takes over a directory they were the last administrator of.

subjectKind.description: A person or a team, as a grant names either.

Task.description:
One thing to work on, whatever tracks it.

The fields are the intersection every tracker has, plus the two that make a
row worth showing: what it is called, and when it last moved.

body.description: Seeds the first prompt, so nobody types the problem out twice.

repo.description: Where the work would happen. Known for an issue; a binding for a ticket.

url.description: Always somewhere to go and read it.

TaskId.description: One subagent run, from the moment it was spawned to its report.

TaskKind.description:
What sort of thing it is.

The one field the Issues/PRs toggle reads, and the reason "filter by kind"
is a query parameter rather than a migration when a second source lands.

TaskScope.description: One thing the list can be narrowed to: a repository, or a team.

key.description: What goes on the wire: `acme/web`, or `ENG`.

everyone.description:
True for the one team that is everybody in the organisation. It has no
membership rows: whoever exists now is who it means.

members.description: How many people are in it. The whole organisation, for `everyone`.

TeamId.description: Identifies a team — a named group of people.

TemporaryPassword.description: What a reset hands back: the new temporary password, said once.

Topic.description: What a client can subscribe to.

connected.description: We hold a credential for it.

keyUrl.description: Where somebody goes to make a key, when that is how it connects.

kinds.description: What this tracker can return, so the kind toggle offers no more.

path.description:
Where that key is filed, and so who else it answers for. Set only
alongside `secret`: the two describe the same shareable thing.

scopeKind.description: Whether the scope picker offers repositories or teams.

secret.description:
The key that answers for this person, as the vault addresses it —
`scope/name/owner`. Absent when nothing is held.

A handle, so a screen can ask who can reach it and offer to file it
somewhere. It is the *resolved* one: their own if they have connected
one, otherwise whatever a directory they work in holds.

images.description:
Pictures pasted or dropped into the composer.

Carried inside the message rather than written to the workspace: there
is nothing to clean up afterwards and no approval prompt for reading a
file somebody just handed over.

oneOf.description: What this session can do, reported once when the agent starts.

mode.description:
What the agent may do without asking, as it reported it.

Read rather than remembered: it is restated at the start of every
turn, so a control showing it is showing what is in force rather
than what was last requested.

detail.description:
Why it ended that way, when the agent said.

A turn that failed used to arrive as a status and nothing else, so
"Your workspace is out of credits. Add credits to continue." — a
sentence the agent had already written, and the only one that would
have explained the silence — was dropped on the floor and the
session read as an agent that had stopped answering for no reason.

oneOf.description:
Set when a subagent owns this item rather than the main thread.

Without it a subagent's tool calls interleave into the transcript
and read as though the main agent made them.

title.description: What the card is called before there is anything in it.

oneOf.description:
Something about an open item changed — usually a tool's arguments
arriving, which come a fragment at a time and are only worth showing
once they parse.
The agent is blocked and cannot continue without an answer.

args.description: The tool's full input, for a card that wants to show more.

detail.description: The command, the path — whatever a person needs to decide.

oneOf.description:
What was decided, when whoever reports it knows.

Codex says only that its request was answered — `serverRequest/
resolved` carries the id and nothing else — so "answered, and it
did not say how" has to be representable. It is the difference
between a card that clears and one that sits on the screen for ever
while somebody presses Allow again.

What the account's own limits say.

Arrives on its own schedule rather than with a turn: a window, whether
we are inside it, and when it starts again. A proportion when the agent
sends one, and nothing drawn from it when it does not — Claude Code
says none, which is why this is optional rather than a number somebody
has to trust.

usedPercent.description:
How much of the window is gone, when the agent says.

Claude Code does not, which is why a bar was not worth drawing.
Codex does, and a window is a far more useful thing to see as a
proportion than as a word.

item.description:
The tool call that spawned it, which is how its items find their way
home.

oneOf.description:
A line we kept but could not name.

Only for what nothing else matched — the complete raw log is already
what Firetower stores, so repeating every mapped line here would double
the volume to say nothing new. This is the marker for "an agent said
something in a shape we have never seen", which is how a version that
grew a new message type shows up as a gap to fill rather than as
silence.

TurnEvent.description:
Something an agent said or did.

The vocabulary the interface draws, and the only thing that crosses out of
the normaliser.

TurnId.description: One exchange: a prompt in, and everything that happened before the agent stopped.

updateAvailable.description: Whether anything at all is behind the newest release.

Updated.description: What one host got out of an update, named so a partial run is readable.

error.description: Why it did not, when it didn't.

version.description: What it has now, when it worked.

UpdaterView.description: The updater beside the control plane, if there is one.

problem.description: Why it cannot be used, in words, when it cannot.

UpgradePlan.description: What a run would do to the deployment's files, asked before agreeing.

envMissing.description: Variables the release's `.env.example` requires that `.env` lacks.

updaterUpgrade.description: Whether the updater itself is behind and will be recreated first.

Usage.description:
What a turn cost, and how much room is left.

Not `Eq`, because the cost is a float. Comparing two of these for equality
is a test convenience, not something to build on.

cacheReadTokens.description: Absent when the agent does not say.

cacheWriteTokens.description:
What was written into the cache on this turn, and billed as such.

Reported apart from what was read because they cost different amounts
and mean different things: reading is the session being cheap, writing
is it having said something new and large.

contextUsed.description:
Everything the model had in front of it on the last request.

Input plus both kinds of cache plus what it wrote. This is the number
that matters to somebody deciding whether a session has room left —
input alone reads as almost nothing once caching is working, which is
exactly when it is least true.

contextWindow.description: How much room the model has at all.

costUsd.description: The agent's own estimate, in dollars. Its arithmetic, not ours.

denied.description: Tools the person refused during the turn.

durationMs.description: How long the turn took, wall clock.

firstTokenMs.description: How long before it said anything.

models.description:
What each model did, when more than one was involved.

A turn is rarely one model: something small names things and summarises
alongside the one doing the work, and it is on the bill. Totals hide
that; this does not.

thinkingTokens.description: Of the output, how much was reasoning rather than answer.

disabled.description: Switched off by an administrator: cannot sign in, keeps what they made.

email.description:
Where to write to them. Absent on accounts made before one was asked
for, and never filled in with a guess: a placeholder address cannot be
told apart from a real one that bounces.

mustChangePassword.description:
True while the password in use was chosen by somebody other than its
owner: out of a file for the first administrator, and by an
administrator for everybody invited or reset since.

Nothing but replacing it is permitted until this clears, and replacing
it is done on the control plane's own interface — the native clients
read this to send people there rather than offering a form of their
own.

slug.description:
The label their own space is named with — the `kevin` in
`u/kevin/ledger_rounding`.

Sent because a client cannot otherwise tell whether a path it is looking
at is *theirs*. "Is this mine" is the first half of "may I decide where
this goes", and a client that has to guess gets it wrong in the generous
direction: it offers a control that the server then refuses.

Not the username. That is chosen by people and may yet become an email
address; this is derived once and never changes, so renaming somebody
never moves anything.

email.description:
An address, for an account made before one was asked for, or when
somebody's has changed.

UserId.description: Identifies someone who can sign in.

brokenAt.description: The first entry that doesn't follow from the one before it, if any.

intact.description: Whether the log's chain of digests still holds end to end.

rootKey.description: Where the key that unlocks all of this lives — in words, never the key.

VoiceState.description: What dictation knows about itself before anybody presses anything.

configured.description: A key is held. Not whether it works — that is only known by using it.

mayConfigure.description: Whether this person may set or replace it. Administrators only.

VoiceTicket.description: A credential for one connection, with about a minute to use it.

expiresAt.description:
When it stops being usable, RFC 3339. Only the connection has to happen
before this; the session it opens outlives it.

session.description:
The `session.update` the client is to send once connected, verbatim.

Handed over rather than left to the client to compose, so that the
settings stay decided in one place — this file — even though it is the
browser that sends them. The client echoes; it does not author.

Sent at all because the documented transcription flow configures the
session after connecting, and whether a pre-configured ephemeral token
also suffices is not something the documentation commits to. Sending it
is idempotent and costs one small frame; not sending it risks the
failure that looks like nothing at all — audio going up, no words
coming back, every layer apparently healthy.

value.description:
The ephemeral client secret, `ek_…`. Not the key, and not a secret this
install stores: it is minted, handed over and forgotten.

WorkSummary.description:
What is in a workspace that isn't safely elsewhere yet.

The thing that makes ending a session a decision rather than a gamble.

commits.description:
Commits on this branch that its base does not have.

Not the same question as `ahead`, which switches to measuring against
the upstream the moment a branch is pushed — so a pushed branch holding
nothing reports `ahead: 0` and looks ready to open a pull request from.
This is what says there is something to open one *for*.

`None` from a worker too old to answer, which is not the same as zero
and must not be drawn as it.

pushed.description: Whether this branch exists on the remote at all.

WorkspaceId.description: Identifies a workspace — the compute a session runs on.

WorkspaceUsage.description:
What one workspace is taking of its machine.

`WorkspaceUsage` rather than `Usage`: [`turn::Usage`] is what a model turn
cost, both cross into one OpenAPI document, and two schemas of one name
there means the second quietly becomes the first — which typed a session's
memory as a count of tokens.

`None` on a session whose worker cannot divide its machine up — an old
worker, a container created without `--privileged`, a host still on cgroup
v1. Absent rather than zero, because "nothing is being measured" and
"nothing is being used" are different things and a meter should not draw
the first as the second.

cpu.description: Cores in use, averaged over the interval between two reports.

memoryMaxMb.description: The ceiling, where there is one.

memoryPeakMb.description:
The high-water mark since the workspace started.

The number worth showing next to a ceiling: what a workspace is using
while its agent thinks says little, and the question behind "how much
does this need" is always about the peak.

oomKills.description:
How many times something in this workspace was killed for going over.

Carried so a session can say so. Without it, a build that vanishes is a
mystery that reads as a crash in whatever was running.
